problems.title: The counted parity orientation depends on length
problems.source_location: Proposition 3, p.6; Appendix A.3, pp.15–16 and final author remark
claim: The proposition claims arbitrary-length parity from two examples with probability \(1-2^{-H}\), counting either opposite-sign transition orientation.
analysis: A coordinate equals \(h_{0,i}(a_i^{[0]})^{T-k}(a_i^{[1]})^k\). Signs \((+,-)\) encode \((-1)^k\), but \((-,+)\) encode \((-1)^T(-1)^k\). For \(H=1,h_0=1\) and independent symmetric Rademacher entries, only \((+,-)\) succeeds for all lengths. The other outcomes have opposite-label hidden-state collisions: \((+,+)\) and \((-,-)\) collide on inputs zero/one, while \((-,+)\) collide on one/one-one. Thus success is \(1/4\), not claimed \(1/2\). With two coordinates \(A_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1),A_1=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)\), training inputs zero-zero/zero-one permit either coordinate readout; only the first extrapolates to odd lengths. Existence therefore does not identify an arbitrary trained readout.
result: The probability and learning interpretation need qualification. The author’s final remark already gives the corrected sufficient-event probability; even-only experimental lengths do not test the unrestricted claim.
repair: Credit the existing author remark: with independent symmetric nonzero entries and nonzero initialization, a selected \((+,-)\) coordinate exists with probability \(1-(3/4)^H\). Known matrices can identify it and two opposite labels orient it. This is a sufficient-event constructive rule, not an exact generic-optimizer probability; fixed length parity separately permits either orientation.
problems.existing_correction_status: The final Appendix A.3 remark already states the appropriate sufficient-event probability. The proposition and unrestricted two-example learning interpretation remain broader.
problems.impact_rationale: This is a bounded theorem/proof mismatch with an explicit existing author qualification; the basic representational capacity and observed even-length results survive.

problems.title: Even orthogonal dimension does not remove reflection blocks
problems.source_location: Section 2.3 and Appendix A.2, rotation-block explanation
claim: The explanation represents an arbitrary even-dimensional real orthogonal matrix entirely by planar rotation blocks.
analysis: Take \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\). It is orthogonal in dimension \(2\) but determinant \(-1\); every rotation-block-only matrix has determinant \(1\), preserved by similarity. The general real form also includes one-dimensional \(+1,-1\) blocks. The paper’s existence construction explicitly chooses rotations, so it does not need the false universal characterization.
result: The canonical-form explanation is overbroad; the cyclic and finite-product representation construction remains valid.
repair: Use the real orthogonal form with \(+1,-1\) eigenspaces and conjugate rotation blocks. For a single even-dimensional determinant-one matrix those real signs can be paired; a family additionally needs a compatible common basis.
problems.existing_correction_status: A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.
problems.impact_rationale: A supporting characterization fails, while the constructive positive theorem does not rely on it.

problems.title: Positive diagonality still permits absorbing-state tracking
problems.source_location: Section 1 hierarchy and Section 2.1 finite-state simulation definition
claim: A parity obstruction should not be interpreted as absence of every nontrivial finite-state tracking task.
analysis: Let the state report whether any one has appeared. With \(h_0=(1,1)\), \(A_0=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1/2)\), \(A_1=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1/4)\), all entries are strictly positive contractions. After length \(T\) with \(k\) ones, \(h_T=2^{-T}(1,2^{-k})\). Scores \(2^{-T-k}\) for unseen-one state and \((3/4)2^{-T}\) for seen-one state classify correctly for \(k=0\) versus \(k\ge1\), including empty input. No additive term or length-aware decoder is used.
result: The broad verbal hierarchy needs narrowing to the forbidden cyclic/group tasks. This exact-arithmetic construction proves neither parity nor robust unlimited-length machine arithmetic nor trainability.
repair: Name the specific excluded tasks and distinguish universal finite-state simulation from particular absorbing-state machines. No complete classification of positive-diagonal automata is supplied.
problems.existing_correction_status: A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.
problems.impact_rationale: A nontrivial absorbing task narrows the explanatory scope; it preserves the actual parity obstruction and empirical comparisons.
